comments.author: @t.espinoza5120
comments.text:
That’s not necessarily a bad idea. If labor costs come down, there’s at least the potential for healthcare costs to come down as well. The bigger problem, in my view, is what happens when government subsidies distort normal market forces.

We’ve seen similar arguments with housing. When government vouchers or subsidized housing guarantee that certain rents can be paid, landlords and property managers have less pressure to lower prices. Meanwhile, working people who earn too much to qualify for assistance but not enough to comfortably afford rising rents can get squeezed the hardest.

College tuition is another example. When large amounts of government-backed financial aid and lending become available, institutions know there is more money available to pay tuition, which can weaken the normal pressure to keep prices competitive.

Healthcare can face some of the same problems. When government, insurance companies, and other third parties are paying much of the bill, the person receiving the service is often disconnected from the actual price.

I’d rather see more genuine competition, price transparency, and market discipline. When businesses actually have to compete for customers who care about what things cost, supply and demand have a much better chance of putting downward pressure on prices.

And when it comes to wages, the argument should be about whether compensation matches the value, skill, responsibility, and market demand for the job, not whether the worker is a man or a woman.
